title: Conditionals
intro: This unit is about **if**. Turkmen needs no separate word for it: the ending `-sA` on the verb does the job (*Wagtyň bolsa, gel*, come if you have time), and *eger* (if) in front is optional. Then come *bolsa* after a participle or a noun, for conditions about what is already so (*gelýän bolsaň*, if you're coming); the **would** of things that are not so (*Wagtym bolsa, gelerdim*, if I had time, I would come); and *kaşki* for **if only** (*Kaşki wagtym bolsa!*). With these four, you have the whole set of Turkmen conditions.

blocks.text: The conditional is the verb stem with `-sA`: *-sa* after a back vowel, *-se* after a front one. Then come the person endings of the past tense ([A2 unit 1](a2-u01)): *-m, -ň*, nothing, *-k, -ňYz, -lAr*. The stem doesn't change before it: no soft *t* (*gitse*), no *e* → *ä* (*işlese*).

rows.en: if he or she doesn't read
if you don't read (plural or polite)

blocks.text: The **if** half comes first, the main clause after it, and the main verb says when: `-Ar` or `-jAk` for the future, the imperative for a request, `-ýAr` for what usually happens. The conditional has no question form of its own: a question goes on the main verb (*Wagtyň bolsa, gelersiňmi?*, will you come if you have time?). *Eger* (if) at the start is optional; it announces the condition early and is common in writing.

items.en: Come if you have time.

items.tk: Eger ertir ýagyş ýagsa, öýde galarys.
items.seg: Eger ertir ýagyş ýag|sa, öý|de gal|ar|ys.
items.en: If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
If you come to Ashgabat, call me.
If we go quickly, we'll catch the train.
If it doesn't rain, we'll go to the park.
When I have time, I read.
items.note: With `-ýAr` in the main clause: whenever it happens.

blocks.text: `-sA` also means **when**, for something you expect: *Ol gelse, bazara gideris*, when (or if) he comes, we'll go to the market. Turkmen doesn't need to choose; English does.

**Suggestions and permission.** On its own, with a question mark, `-sA` makes a gentle suggestion: *Biraz dynç alsaň?* (how about a little rest?), *Bile gitsek?* (shall we go together?). With *bolýarmy?* it asks permission, as you saw in [A2 unit 5](a2-u05): *Girsem bolýarmy?*, literally **if I come in, is it all right?** And *mümkin bolsa* is **if possible**: *Mümkin bolsa, ertir geliň*.

blocks.title: ýogsa: or else
blocks.text: *Ýogsa* (otherwise, or else) turns a condition around: it means **if not**. *Çalt bol, ýogsa gijä galarys* (hurry up, or else we'll be late) says the same as *Çalt bolmasaň, gijä galarys*.

blocks.title: Past endings, not -sYn
blocks.text: The endings are those of *geldim, geldik*: *gelsem, gelsek*, not `gelserin` or `gelseris`. And keep `-sA` apart from `-sYn` ([A2 unit 7](a2-u07)): *gelse* is **if he comes**, *gelsin* is **let him come**.

sections.title: If it's so: bolsa after participles and nouns

blocks.text: Plain `-sA` is for something that may happen: *ertir gelseň*, if you come tomorrow. When the condition is about what is **already** so, or already planned or done, Turkmen puts it in a participle or a noun and adds *bolsa*, the conditional of *bolmak* (to be), with the person ending: *gelýän bolsaň*, if you're coming (if that's the case).

The participle and the noun don't change; the person goes on *bolsa*. For **not**, use the negative participles of [B1 unit 6](b1-u06), `-mAýAn`, `-mAdYk`, `-mAjAk`, or *däl* after a noun or adjective. With **have**, the thing you have is the subject, so *bolsa* stays in the third person and the possessive says whose: *wagtyň bolsa* (if you have time), *pulum ýok bolsa* (if I have no money).

rows.en: if he or she is coming

items.tk: Mara gidýän bolsaň, maňa bir gawun getir.
items.seg: Mar|a gid|ýän bol|sa|ň, maňa bir gawun getir.
items.en: If you're going to Mary, bring me a melon.

items.tk: Mara gitjek bolsaňyz, otly bilen gidiň.
items.seg: Mar|a git|jek bol|sa|ňyz, otly bilen gid|iň.
items.en: If you're going to go to Mary, go by train.
If you've read the book, give it to me.

items.tk: Ol eýýäm giden bolsa, ertir oňa jaň ederin.
items.seg: Ol eýýäm gid|en bol|sa, ertir oňa jaň ed|er|in.
items.en: If he has already left, I'll call him tomorrow.
If you're hungry, eat something.

items.tk: Öýde hiç kim ýok bolsa, maňa jaň et.
items.seg: Öý|de hiç kim ýok bol|sa, maňa jaň et.
items.en: If nobody is at home, call me.

blocks.title: Plain -sA or bolsa?
blocks.text: *Ertir gelseň, jaň et*: if you come tomorrow (you may or may not), call. *Ertir gelýän bolsaň, jaň et*: if you're coming tomorrow (if that's the plan), call. English often uses the same words for both; Turkmen asks whether the condition is a possibility or something you're checking.

blocks.title: The other bolsa: as for
blocks.text: Right after a subject, with the sentence going on to its own verb, *bolsa* means **as for**, **while**: *Men öýde galaryn, Aýna bolsa işe gider* (I'll stay at home; Aýna, for her part, will go to work). Look at the word before it: a participle or a predicate (*gelýän bolsa*, *öýde bolsa*) makes it **if**.

sections.title: If I were you: things that are not so

blocks.text: For a condition you know is not true, keep `-sA` in the **if** half and put the main verb in `-ArdY`, the **used to** form of [B1 unit 2](b1-u02), which here means **would**: *Wagtym bolsa, gelerdim*, if I had time, I would come (but I don't). For the past, put the **if** half in `-An bolsa`: *Wagtym bolan bolsa, gelerdim*, if I had had time, I would have come.

The main verb is the same `-ArdY` for now and for the past; the **if** half, or the context, tells you which. A question puts *-my* before `-dY`, as in [B1 unit 2](b1-u02): *Sen näme ederdiň?*, *Gelermidiň?* (would you come?). And *-(Y)p bilerdi* gives **could**: *Ir çykan bolsaň, ýetişip bilerdiň*, if you had left early, you could have made it.

items.en: If I had money, I would buy a new car.

items.tk: Men seniň ýeriňde bolsam, oňa jaň ederdim.
items.seg: Men seniň ýer|iň|de bol|sa|m, oňa jaň ed|er|di|m.
items.en: If I were you, I would call her.
If it weren't raining, we would go to the park.
If I had got up early, I would have caught the train.
If I had known, I would have told you.

items.tk: Ol jaň etmedik bolsa, men bilmezdim.
items.seg: Ol jaň et|me|dik bol|sa, men bil|mez|di|m.
items.en: If he hadn't called, I wouldn't have known.

blocks.text: `-ArdY` can also stand without an **if**. It softens a wish or a guess: *Bu gowy bolardy* (that would be good); and with *ýöne* (but) it says what you would have done: *Men maşyn alardym, ýöne pulum ýetmedi* (I would have bought a car, but I didn't have enough money).

blocks.title: Used to, or would?
blocks.text: *Gelerdim* is both **I used to come** and **I would come**. With an **if** half or *ýöne* after it, it is **would**: *Wagtym bolsa, gelerdim*. With *öň*, *her gün* or *çagakam*, it is **used to**: *Çagakam her gün gelerdim*.

blocks.title: Real or not?
blocks.text: *Wagtym bolsa, gelerin*: I may have time, and then I'll come. *Wagtym bolsa, gelerdim*: I don't have time, so I won't. The **if** half is the same; the main verb tells the listener whether you think it can happen.

*Kaşki* opens a wish: **if only**, **I wish**. The verb that follows is in `-sA`: *Kaşki wagtym bolsa!* (if only I had time!), *Kaşki ýagyş ýagsa!* (if only it would rain!). For the past, a regret, use `-An bolsa`, as in the section above: *Kaşki ir turan bolsam!* (if only I had got up early!).

blocks.caption: Wishes with *kaşki*
head: Turkmen
English
rows: Kaşki sen hem bu ýerde bolsaň!
I wish you were here too!
If only she would come too!
If only it doesn't rain tomorrow!
Kaşki men muny öň bilen bolsam!
If only I had known this before!
I wish I hadn't told him!

items.en: If only it would rain!
I wish I hadn't gone!
If only I had got up early!
If only I had money, I would travel.

blocks.text: A wish can stand alone, with an exclamation mark, or lead into what would follow, with `-ArdY` as in the last example. For a hope that may come true, Turkmen also says *umyt edýärin* (I hope): *Umyt edýärin, ertir ýagyş ýagmaz*.

blocks.title: In books: -sAdY
blocks.text: In written Turkmen you will also meet `-sA` followed by the past `-dY`, for a wish that can no longer come true. Grammars give it in two shapes, *alsadym* and *ýazsamdym*, with the person ending once or twice. This course says the same thing with `-An bolsa`: *Kaşki bilen bolsam!*

blocks.title: kaşki takes -sA
blocks.text: *Kaşki gelse!*, not `Kaşki geldi!` For a regret about the past, keep `-sA` on *bolmak*: *Kaşki gelen bolsa!*

lines.tk: Şenbe güni näme edýärsiň? Wagtyň bolsa, daga gideli.
lines.en: What are you doing on Saturday? If you have time, let's go to the mountains.

lines.tk: Howa gowy bolsa, gelerin. Howa maglumatyny gördüňmi?
lines.en: If the weather's good, I'll come. Have you seen the forecast?

lines.tk: Hawa. Howa maglumatyna görä, şenbe güni ýagyş ýagar.
lines.en: Yes. According to the forecast, it'll rain on Saturday.

lines.tk: Onda ýekşenbe gitsek? Ýagyş ýagmasa, irden ugrarys.
lines.en: Then how about Sunday? If it doesn't rain, we'll set off in the morning.

lines.tk: Bolýar. Kaşki Batyr hem gelse! Ol gelse, maşyn bilen giderdik.
lines.en: OK. If only Batyr would come too! If he came, we'd go by car.

lines.tk: Men seniň ýeriňde bolsam, oňa häzir jaň ederdim.
lines.en: If I were you, I'd call him now.
You're right. I'll call him now!

summary: **If**: `-sA` with the past endings (*gelsem, gelseň, gelse, gelsek, gelseňiz, gelseler*); negative `-mAsA` (*gelmesem*). *Eger* in front is optional.
The **if** half comes first; the main verb says when: *Wagtyň bolsa, gel*; *Ýagyş ýagsa, öýde galarys*.
On its own, `-sA` suggests or asks: *Biraz dynç alsaň?*, *Girsem bolýarmy?*
For what is already so, a participle or a noun with *bolsa*: *gelýän bolsaň, gitjek bolsaň, okan bolsaň, öýde bolsaň*.
For what is not so: `-sA …, -ArdY` (*Wagtym bolsa, gelerdim*); for the past, `-An bolsa …, -ArdY` (*Ir turan bolsam, ýetişerdim*).
*Kaşki* with `-sA` is **if only**: *Kaşki wagtym bolsa!*; for a regret, *Kaşki ir turan bolsam!*
*Bolsa* right after a subject means **as for**: *Aýna bolsa işe gider*.
